en: Vibhaṅga:
Analysis of the Jhānas 1.
Suttantabhājanīya (The Exposition According to the Discourses)
Here, a bhikkhu dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults;

he trains himself by undertaking the rules of training; he guards the doors of his sense faculties, is moderate in eating, and is devoted to the practice of wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night, being constant and discerning in regard to the states conducive to enlightenment.
He is devoted to the practice of meditation.
He acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning; he acts with clear comprehension when looking ahead and looking aside;
he acts with clear comprehension when bending and stretching his limbs; he acts with clear comprehension when wearing his outer robe, bowl, and inner robes.
He acts with clear comprehension when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; he acts with clear comprehension in discharging excrement and urine;
he acts with clear comprehension in going, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and remaining silent.
He resorts to a secluded lodging: a forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, or a remote jungle thicket.
A forest grove, an open space, a heap of straw— quiet, free from noise, secluded from people,
a place for private retreat suitable for seclusion.
Having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, he sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
Thus, having abandoned covetousness for the world, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness; he purifies his mind of covetousness.
Having abandoned ill will and hatred, he dwells with a mind free from ill will, compassionate for the welfare of all living beings; he purifies his mind of ill will and hatred.
Having abandoned sloth and torpor, he dwells free from sloth and torpor, percipient of light, mindful and clearly comprehending; he purifies his mind of sloth and torpor.
Having abandoned restlessness and remorse, he dwells unagitated, with a mind inwardly calmed; he purifies his mind of restlessness and remorse.
Having abandoned doubt, he dwells as one who has crossed beyond doubt, free from uncertainty regarding wholesome states; he purifies his mind of doubt.
Having abandoned these five hindrances—defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—and being secluded from sensual pleasures...
Secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.

With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and mental unification, is without applied and sustained thought, and possesses rapture and pleasure born of concentration.
With the fading away of rapture, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness with the body;
he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the Noble Ones declare: “He dwells happily, mindful and equanimous.

With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.

With the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, [thinking] "space is infinite," one enters and dwells in the base of infinite space;
by completely surmounting the base of infinite space, [thinking] "consciousness is infinite," one enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness;
by completely surmounting the base of infinite consciousness, [thinking] "there is nothing," one enters and dwells in the base of nothingness.
Having completely transcended the base of nothingness, he enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This is the matrix (*mātikā*). "Here" refers to this view, this inclination, this preference, this adoption, and this...
In this Dhamma, in this Vinaya, in this Dhamma-Vinaya, in this teaching, in this holy life,
in this instruction of the Teacher.
Therefore it is called "here."
“Bhikkhu”: a bhikkhu by convention; a bhikkhu by profession; a bhikkhu because he begs; a bhikkhu because he is a beggar;
a bhikkhu because he has entered upon the way of begging; a bhikkhu because he wears torn robes;
a bhikkhu because he breaks evil, unwholesome states; a bhikkhu because of the breaking of evil, unwholesome states.
A bhikkhu through the specific abandonment of defilements; a bhikkhu through the non-specific abandonment of defilements;
a bhikkhu in training; a bhikkhu beyond training; a bhikkhu who is neither in training nor beyond training; a bhikkhu who is supreme; a bhikkhu who is excellent;

a bhikkhu who is refined; a bhikkhu who is essential; and one who has been [ordained] by a unanimous Saṅgha through a formal act consisting of a motion and a third proclamation, which is irreversible and fit for the occasion.
One who has received full ordination is a *bhikkhu*.
“*Pātimokkha*” means virtue; it is the foundation, the beginning, the conduct, the restraint, the control, and the liberation—the foremost—for the attainment of wholesome states.
“*Saṃvara*” (restraint) means non-transgression regarding the body, non-transgression regarding speech, and non-transgression regarding both body and speech.
“Restrained” (*saṃvuta*) means that he is endowed with, fully endowed with, arrived at, fully arrived at, possessed of, perfected in, and equipped with the restraint of the Pātimokkha.
Therefore, he is called “restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha.
“Dwells” (*viharati*) means he moves about, conducts himself, protects, maintains, sustains, fares along, and abides.
Therefore it is said, “he dwells.
Regarding the phrase “endowed with proper conduct and resort”: there is proper conduct and there is improper conduct.
In this context, what is improper conduct?
Transgression by body, transgression by speech, and transgression by both body and speech—
this is called "improper conduct.
Furthermore, all immorality is improper conduct.
Here, someone makes a living by means of giving bamboo, or giving bowls, or giving flowers, or giving fruits, or giving bath-powder,
or giving tooth-sticks; or by flattery, or by bean-soupery, or by servility, or by running errands on foot,
or by some other kind of wrong livelihood censured by the Buddha.
This is called "improper conduct.
In this regard, what is proper conduct?
It is non-transgression by way of body, non-transgression by way of speech, and non-transgression by way of both body and speech.
This is called "conduct" (ācāra).
All restraint of virtue (sīlasaṃvara) is conduct.
Here, a certain person does not [give] gifts of bamboo, nor gifts of leaves, nor gifts of flowers, nor gifts of fruits, nor gifts of bathing.
One does not maintain one's livelihood by giving tooth-sticks, nor by flattery, nor by "mung-bean soup" behavior, nor by servility, nor by running errands on foot,
nor by any other kind of wrong livelihood censured by the Buddha—
this is called "proper conduct."
“Range”: there is a proper range and there is an improper range.
In this regard, what is the improper range?
Here, someone has prostitutes as his range, or widows as his range, or unmarried girls as his range, or eunuchs as his range.
Whether it be the domain of nuns or the domain of taverns, he dwells in association with kings,
royal ministers, members of other sects, and the disciples of those sects, through improper association;
or else he frequents those families that are faithless, lacking confidence, unrefuge-like, and prone to reviling and abuse.

To frequent, associate with, and attend upon families that desire what is unbeneficial, what is harmful, what is uncomfortable, and what is not the security from bondage for monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—
this is called "an improper resort."
In this regard, what is the proper resort?
Here, a certain person does not frequent prostitutes as a resort, nor widows, nor unmarried girls, nor eunuchs, nor bhikkhunīs, nor taverns;
he dwells unassociated with kings and royal ministers.
Through unwholesome association with those of other sects and their disciples;
or rather, through association with those families that are faithful and confident, which serve as wellsprings for the saffron-robed, which are fragrant with the scent of sages,
and which desire the welfare, benefit, comfort, and security of the bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
He frequents, associates with, and attends upon such families of female lay disciples—this is called "the resort.
Thus, he is endowed with this conduct and this resort... [as above] ...possessed of them.
Therefore, he is called "one perfected in conduct and resort.
Regarding the phrase "seeing fear in even the slightest faults":
therein, what are the slightest faults?
Those faults which are trifling, minor, slight, and considered slight, which require restraint, require self-control, require the arising of a thought,
and are dependent upon attention— these are called "slight faults.
Thus, regarding these slight faults, he is one who sees the fault, sees the danger, sees the disadvantage, and sees the escape.
Therefore it is said: “Seeing fear in even the slightest faults.
“Having undertaken them, he trains in the rules of training.
In this context, what is training?

There are four trainings: the training for bhikkhus is the bhikkhu-training; the training for bhikkhunīs is the bhikkhunī-training; the training for upāsakas is the upāsaka-training; the training for upāsikās is the upāsikā-training.
These are called "trainings."
Thus, he conducts himself by undertaking these trainings in their entirety, in every way, completely, without remainder, and without exception.
Therefore, it is said: “He trains by undertaking the rules of training.

Regarding the phrase “guarding the doors of the sense faculties,” there is the state of guarding the doors of the sense faculties, and there is the state of not guarding the doors of the sense faculties.
In this regard, what is the lack of restraint of the sense faculties?
Here, someone, having seen a form with the eye, grasps at its general appearance and grasps at its secondary details.
Because he dwells with that faculty of the eye unrestrained, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—arise.
If, upon seeing a form with the eye, there should arise in him covetousness, dejection, or evil unwholesome states, which might overwhelm his mind, he does not practice for its restraint;
he does not guard the faculty of the eye, nor does he achieve restraint over the faculty of the eye.
Upon hearing a sound with the ear... [and so on].
Having smelled an odor with the nose …pe… having tasted a flavor with the tongue …pe… having touched a tangible object with the body …pe…
Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he grasps at its signs and grasps at its secondary characteristics.

Since covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might flow in upon one who dwells with this faculty of mind unrestrained, he does not practice for its restraint; he does not guard the faculty of mind regarding the faculty of mind.
One does not attain restraint.
That which is the lack of guarding, the lack of protection, the lack of preservation, and the lack of restraint regarding these six faculties—
this is called "unrestrainedness of the doors of the faculties."
In this regard, what is restraint of the sense-doors?
Here, someone, having seen a form with the eye, does not grasp at its general appearance nor grasp at its secondary details.
For if one dwells with the eye-faculty unrestrained, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might arise.

If, when he has seen a form with the eye, there should arise in him states that are covetous and deplorable, states that lead to bondage; if, when he has heard a sound with the ear... [and so on] ...if, when he has smelled an odor with the nose... [and so on] ...states that would flow in after him, he practices for its restraint, guards the faculty of the eye, and achieves restraint over the faculty of the eye. Having heard a sound with the ear... [and so on] ...having smelled an odor with the nose... [and so on] ...he practices for its restraint, guards the faculty of the nose, and achieves restraint over the faculty of the nose.
Having tasted a flavor with the tongue … having touched a tangible object with the body … having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind,
he does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.
Knowing this danger—that if one dwells with the faculty of the mind unguarded, covetousness and dejection, evil and unwholesome states, might flow in upon him—one practices for its restraint;
he guards the faculty of the mind and attains restraint over the faculty of the mind.
This guarding, protecting, shielding, and restraint of these six faculties—this is [called] restraint.
This is called "guarding the doors of the sense faculties.
One is endowed with, fully endowed with, ...pe... possessed of this guarding of the doors of the sense faculties.
Therefore it is said: "One who guards the doors of the sense-faculties.
Regarding "moderation in eating": there is moderation in eating, and there is lack of moderation in eating.
In this regard, what is lack of moderation in eating?
Here, someone without reflection and without wise consideration partakes of food for the sake of amusement, intoxication, adornment, and embellishment.
Whatever lack of contentment, lack of moderation, and lack of reflection there is regarding food—
that is called "immoderation in eating."
In this regard, what is moderation in eating? Here,
someone reflects wisely and takes food,
neither for amusement, nor for intoxication, nor for the sake of physical beauty or ornamentation, but only for the maintenance and sustenance of this body.
“For the sake of maintaining this body, for the cessation of harm, and for the support of the holy life, thinking:
‘Thus I shall terminate old feelings and not give rise to new feelings, and there will be for me sustenance, blamelessness, and a comfortable dwelling.
That which therein is contentment, moderation, and reflection upon food.”
This is called "moderation in eating.
One who is endowed with this moderation in eating... [as before] ...is possessed of it.
Therefore, one is called "one who knows the measure in food."
And how is a bhikkhu devoted to the practice of wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night?
Here, a bhikkhu purifies his mind from obstructive states by means of walking and sitting during the day;
he purifies his mind from obstructive states by means of walking and sitting during the first watch of the night.
During the middle watch of the night, he lies down on his right side in the lion’s posture,
placing one foot upon the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, having fixed his mind on the perception of rising. During the last watch of the night, having risen,
he purifies his mind from obstructive states by means of walking and sitting.
In this way, a bhikkhu is devoted to the practice of wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night.
"Constancy" refers to that arousal of mental energy which is right effort.
“Skillfulness” means:
that which is wisdom, understanding ... [as before] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view.
“Devoted to the practice of developing the states conducive to enlightenment.”
In this context, what are the states conducive to enlightenment?
They are the seven factors of enlightenment:

the mindfulness factor of enlightenment, the investigation-of-phenomena factor of enlightenment, the energy factor of enlightenment, the rapture factor of enlightenment, the tranquility factor of enlightenment, the concentration factor of enlightenment, and the equanimity factor of enlightenment.
These are called "the states conducive to enlightenment.
Thus, one cultivates, develops, and makes much of those states conducive to enlightenment.
Therefore, it is said: "one is devoted to the practice of the development of the states conducive to enlightenment."
And how does a bhikkhu act with clear comprehension when going forward and returning; act with clear comprehension when looking ahead and looking aside;
act with clear comprehension when bending and stretching his limbs; act with clear comprehension when wearing his outer robe, inner robe, and bowl;
act with clear comprehension when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; and act with clear comprehension when defecating and urinating?
How does he act with clear comprehension when going, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and remaining silent?

Here, a monk acts with mindfulness and clear comprehension when stepping forward; he acts with mindfulness and clear comprehension when stepping back; he acts with mindfulness and clear comprehension when looking ahead;

he acts with mindfulness and clear comprehension when looking aside; he acts with mindfulness and clear comprehension when bending his limbs; he acts with mindfulness and clear comprehension when stretching them out.
He acts with mindfulness and clear comprehension; he acts with mindfulness and clear comprehension in carrying his outer robe, bowl, and robes;
he acts with mindfulness and clear comprehension in eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; he acts with mindfulness and clear comprehension in defecating and urinating;
he acts with mindfulness and clear comprehension in going, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and remaining silent.
In this context, what is mindfulness?

That which is mindfulness, constant mindfulness, clear mindfulness, mindfulness, the state of remembering, the state of bearing in mind, the state of not losing, the state of not forgetting, mindfulness, the faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, and right mindfulness— this is called "mindfulness."
“Clearly comprehending”: therein, what is clear comprehension?

It is that which is wisdom, understanding, investigation, thorough investigation, investigation of phenomena, discernment, close examination, detailed examination, sagacity, skill, proficiency, discrimination, reflection, scrutiny, breadth, intelligence, guidance, insight.
Clear comprehension is the goad; it is wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the sword of wisdom, the palace of wisdom, the light of wisdom,
the radiance of wisdom, the lamp of wisdom, the jewel of wisdom, non-delusion, the investigation of phenomena, and right view—
this is called "clear comprehension."
Thus, he is endowed with this mindfulness and this clear comprehension … [as before] … possessed of them.
In this way, a bhikkhu goes forward mindfully and clearly comprehending, goes backward mindfully and clearly comprehending;

he looks ahead mindfully and clearly comprehending, looks aside mindfully and clearly comprehending; he bends his limbs mindfully and clearly comprehending, extends his limbs mindfully and clearly comprehending.
He acts with mindfulness and clear comprehension; he acts with mindfulness and clear comprehension in carrying his outer robe, bowl, and robes;
he acts with mindfulness and clear comprehension in eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; he acts with mindfulness and clear comprehension in defecating and urinating;
he acts with clear comprehension in going, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and remaining silent.
“Secluded”: even if the lodging is near, it is secluded if it is not crowded with householders and those who have gone forth;
by that it is secluded.
Even if the lodging is far away, it is secluded if it is not crowded with householders and those who have gone forth.
Therefore, it is secluded.

"Recluse's lodging" (senāsana) means: a bed is a recluse's lodging, a chair is a recluse's lodging, a mattress is a recluse's lodging, a pillow is a recluse's lodging, a monastery (vihāra) is a recluse's lodging, a gabled house (aḍḍhayoga) is a recluse's lodging, a mansion (pāsāda) is a recluse's lodging, a watchtower (aṭṭa) is a recluse's lodging... [and so forth].
A dwelling is a lodging; a multi-storied building is a lodging; a cave is a lodging; a grotto is a lodging; the foot of a tree is a lodging;
a bamboo thicket is a lodging.
Or wherever monks retire, all that is a lodging.
“He resorts to a secluded lodging”: he resorts to, frequents, uses, dwells upon, and cultivates this secluded lodging.
Therefore it is said, “he resorts to a secluded lodging.
“The forest”: having gone out beyond the threshold post, all that is the forest.
“Root of a tree”: the root of a tree itself is the “root of a tree.
A mountain itself is a “mountain.
A cave itself is a “cave.”
A mountain cave is indeed a mountain cave;
a charnel ground is indeed a charnel ground;
an open space is indeed an open space.
"A heap of straw is indeed like a heap of straw.
"Forest retreats" is a designation for remote lodgings;
"forest retreats" is a designation for lodgings in forest thickets.
“Forest-dwelling” is a designation for terrifying lodgings;
“forest-dwelling” is a designation for hair-raising lodgings;
“forest-dwelling” is a designation for remote lodgings.
“Forest-dwelling” (*vanapattha*) is a designation for lodgings that are not within the vicinity of human habitation.
“Forest-dwelling” is a designation for lodgings that are difficult to access.
“Quiet” means that even if the lodging is near [a village], it is not crowded with householders or those who have gone forth.
Because of that, it is quiet.
Even if the lodging is far away, provided it is not crowded with householders and renunciants,
because of that, it is quiet.
“With little noise”: that which has little sound is itself that which has little clamor;
that which has little clamor is itself free from the breath of people;
that which is free from the breath of people is itself secluded from human beings.
Whatever is secluded from human beings is indeed suitable for seclusion.
“Having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut”: he has gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut.
“Sits down, folding his legs crosswise”: he sits down, having folded his legs crosswise.
“Having set the body erect”: the body is straight, established, and poised.
“Having established mindfulness directed toward the front”: therein, what is mindfulness?
That which is mindfulness, recollection, constant recollection … [and so on] … right mindfulness.
This is called "mindfulness.
This mindfulness is established, well-established, either at the tip of the nose or on the feature of the mouth.
Therefore it is said: "having established mindfulness directed toward the face."
“Having abandoned covetousness for the world”: therein, what is covetousness?
That which is lust, infatuation …pe… infatuation of the mind—this is called “covetousness.”
In this context, what is the world?
The five aggregates of clinging are the world;
this is called "the world."
This covetousness, in this world, has become stilled, calmed, subsided, come to an end, utterly vanished, dissolved, fully dissolved, withered away, completely withered away, and brought to an end.
Therefore it is said: "having abandoned covetousness for the world.
Regarding the phrase "with a mind free from covetousness," what therein is "mind"?
That which is consciousness, mind, mentation … [as above] … the corresponding element of mind-consciousness—
this is called "consciousness.
This consciousness is free from covetousness.
Therefore it is said: "with a mind free from covetousness.
"Dwells" means: he conducts himself, proceeds, protects, maintains, sustains, moves about, and dwells.
Therefore it is said: "he dwells."
“He purifies the mind of covetousness. In this context, what is covetousness?
Whatever lust, infatuation, ...pe... infatuation of the mind—that is called “covetousness.”
In this context, what is consciousness?
That which is consciousness, mind, mentation … [as before] … the corresponding element of mind-consciousness—
this is called "consciousness."
This mind he cleanses, purifies, thoroughly cleanses, liberates, releases, and completely releases from covetousness.
Therefore it is said: "He purifies the mind of covetousness.
Regarding the phrase "having abandoned ill will and malice": there is ill will, and there is malice.
In this context, what is ill will (*byāpāda*)?
It is the resentment, hostility, antagonism, and opposition of the mind; anger, provocation, and intense provocation; hatred, malice, and intense malice;
the corruption of the mind, mental corruption, wrath, being angry, the state of being angry; hatred, hating, the state of hating.
Ill will, malice, the state of being malicious, hostility, antagonism, ferocity, abruptness, and mental dissatisfaction—
this is called "ill will" (*byāpāda*).
In this context, what is "corruption" (*padosa*)?
Whatever is ill will is malice, and whatever is malice is ill will.
Thus this ill will and this malice have become stilled, calmed, subsided, ceased, vanished, dissolved, fully dissolved, withered away, completely withered away, and brought to an end.
Therefore it is said: "having abandoned ill will and malice."
“With a mind free from ill will”: therein, what is the mind?
That which is mind, mentality, mentation … [as above] … the corresponding element of mind-consciousness—this is called “mind.”
This mind is free from ill will.
Therefore it is said, "one whose mind is free from ill will.
"Dwells" ... [and so on] ...
Therefore it is said, "he dwells.
"He purifies the mind of ill will and malice":
there is ill will, and there is malice.
In this context, what is ill will?
It is the resentment of the mind...
[as before] ...the ferocity, the irritability, the displeasure of the mind.
This is called ill will (*vyāpāda*).
In this context, what is malice (*padosa*)?
That which is ill will is malice; that which is malice is ill will.
In this context, what is consciousness?
That which is consciousness, mind, mentation …pe… the element of mind-consciousness born thereof—
this is called "consciousness."
This mind he cleanses, purifies, thoroughly cleanses, liberates, releases, and completely liberates from ill will and hatred.
Therefore it is said: “He cleanses the mind of ill will and hatred.
Regarding the phrase “having abandoned dullness and drowsiness”: there is dullness, and there is drowsiness.
In this context, what is sloth?

That which is the mind’s lack of health, lack of wieldiness, sluggishness, lingering, being sluggish, the state of being sluggish, sloth, the tendency toward sloth, the state of being slothful within the mind—
this is called "sloth."
In this context, what is torpor?
That which is the body’s lack of fitness, lack of pliability, constriction, envelopment, internal obstruction, torpor, drowsiness, nodding, sleep, sleeping,
the state of being sleepy— this is called “torpor.”
Thus, this sloth and this torpor have become stilled, calmed, subsided, passed away, vanished, dissolved, fully dissolved, withered, utterly withered, and brought to an end.
Therefore it is said: "having abandoned sloth and torpor," and "one who is free from sloth and torpor."
Because that sloth and torpor have been abandoned, vomited out, released, relinquished, and utterly cast off—therefore it is said, "one who is free from sloth and torpor.
"Dwells" ... [as before] ...
Therefore it is said, “he dwells.
Regarding the phrase “perceiving light”:
what therein is perception?
Whatever is perception, perceiving, the state of having perceived—
this is called "perception.
This perception is luminous, open, pure, and radiant.
Therefore it is said: "possessing the perception of light.
"Mindful and clearly comprehending.
In this context, what is mindfulness?
That which is mindfulness, recollection... [and so on] ...right mindfulness—this is called “mindfulness.
In this context, what is clear comprehension?
That wisdom which is understanding … [as before] … non-delusion, the investigation of phenomena, right view—
this is called “clear comprehension.
Thus, he is possessed of this mindfulness and this clear comprehension … [as before] … endowed with them.
Therefore it is said: "mindful and clearly comprehending.
"He purifies the mind of sloth and torpor":
there is sloth, and there is torpor.
In this context, what is sloth?
… [as before] … This is called sloth.
In this context, what is torpor? … [as before] …
This is called "torpor.
In this context, what is "mind"? ...
[as before] ... this is called "mind."
This mind he cleanses, purifies, thoroughly cleanses, liberates, releases, and completely releases from this sloth and torpor.
Therefore it is said: "He thoroughly cleanses the mind of sloth and torpor.
Regarding the phrase "having abandoned restlessness and remorse": there is restlessness, and there is remorse.
In this context, what is restlessness?
That which is restlessness of mind, lack of tranquility, mental agitation, and instability of mind—
this is called "restlessness."
In this context, what is worry?

Perception of what is unallowable as allowable, perception of what is allowable as unallowable, perception of what is blameless as blameworthy, perception of what is blameworthy as blameless; that which is such worry, the state of worrying, the act of worrying, remorse of mind, mental scruple—this is called "worry."
Thus, this restlessness and this remorse have become stilled, calmed, subsided, come to an end, passed away, dissolved, vanished, withered, utterly dried up, and brought to an end.
Therefore it is said: "having abandoned restlessness and remorse.

"Unrestless" means that because of the abandoning, the vomiting out, the being freed from, the relinquishing, and the renouncing of that restlessness and remorse—having both abandoned and renounced them.
Therefore it is said, “unagitated.
“Dwells” … [as before] … therefore it is said, “dwells.”
“With a mind calmed. In this context, what is the mind?
That which is mind, mentality, mentation … [and so on] … the corresponding element of mind-consciousness.
This is called "the mind.
This mind is internally calmed, stilled, and tranquilized.
Therefore, it is said: "one whose mind is internally tranquilized."
“He purifies the mind of restlessness and remorse”: there is restlessness, and there is remorse.
In this context, what is restlessness?
That which is the restlessness of the mind, the lack of tranquility, the distraction of the mind, the wavering of the mind.
This is called "restlessness.
In that regard, what is "worry"? ... [as before] ...
this is called "worry."
In this context, what is consciousness? ... [as before] ...
this is called "consciousness.
This consciousness purifies, cleanses, thoroughly cleanses, liberates, releases, and completely releases itself from this restlessness and remorse.
Therefore it is said: “He purifies the mind of restlessness and worry.
Regarding the phrase “having abandoned doubt”: therein, what is doubt?

It is that which is perplexity, state of being perplexed, state of having been perplexed, uncertainty, doubt, hesitation, bifurcation of the path, wavering, holding to various sides, sliding back and forth, lack of penetration, trepidation of the mind, and mental distress.
This is called "doubt.
This doubt has become stilled, calmed, subsided, come to an end, utterly vanished, ceased, dissolved, withered away, completely dried up, and brought to an end.
Therefore, it is said: "having abandoned doubt."
“Crossed over doubt”: he has crossed over this doubt, has gone beyond it, has emerged from it, has reached the further shore, has attained the further shore.
Therefore, he is called “one who has crossed over doubt.

“Without perplexity regarding wholesome states”: because of this absence of doubt, he does not hesitate, does not doubt regarding wholesome states; he is without perplexity, free from perplexity, and devoid of perplexity.
Therefore it is said: “He is free from doubt regarding wholesome states.
Regarding the phrase “he purifies the mind of doubt,” what therein is doubt?
It is that which is perplexity, the state of being perplexed, the condition of being perplexed, agitation of the mind, and mental distress.
This is called "doubt.
In this context, what is consciousness?
That which is consciousness, mind, mentation … [as before] … the corresponding element of mind-consciousness.
This is called "the mind.
One cleanses, purifies, thoroughly purifies, liberates, releases, and completely releases this mind from this doubt.
Therefore, it is said: "one thoroughly purifies the mind of doubt."
“Having abandoned these five hindrances”: these five hindrances have become stilled, calmed, subsided, ceased, vanished, dissolved, dispelled, withered, utterly withered, and brought to an end.
Therefore it is said, “having abandoned these five hindrances.
“Corruptions of the mind”: these five hindrances are the corruptions of the mind.
“Regarding ‘the weakening of wisdom’ (*paññāya dubbalīkaraṇe*): by means of these five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), both unarisen wisdom does not arise, and arisen wisdom ceases.
Therefore it is said, ‘the weakening of wisdom.
Regarding the phrase ‘quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states’: therein, what are sensual pleasures?”

Desire as will is sensual pleasure; lust is sensual pleasure; desire-and-lust is sensual pleasure; intention is sensual pleasure; passion is sensual pleasure; intention-and-passion is sensual pleasure—these are called "sensual pleasures.
In this context, what are unwholesome states?
Sensual desire, ill will, sloth, torpor, restlessness, remorse, and doubt—
these are called unwholesome states.
Thus, he is secluded from these sensual pleasures and these unwholesome states.
Therefore it is said: “Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states.
“With applied thought and sustained thought”: there is applied thought (vitakka) and there is sustained thought (vicāra).
In this context, what is applied thought?
Whatever is thought, initial application, intention, absorption, sustained application, the directing of the mind, and right intention—
this is called "thought" (vitakka).
In that regard, what is "sustained application" (vicāra)?

Whatever is initial mental application (*vitakka*), sustained mental application (*vicāra*), close examination (*anuvicāra*), detailed scrutiny (*upavicāra*), the continuous threading of the mind, and the repeated inspection—this is called "sustained mental application" (*vicāra*).
Thus, he is endowed with this initial mental application and this sustained mental application... [as before] ...possessed of them.
Therefore it is said, "with applied thought and sustained thought.
"Born of seclusion" means that applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, happiness,
and one-pointedness of mind are born, produced, brought forth, fully manifested, and made apparent in this seclusion.
Therefore it is said, "born of seclusion.
Regarding "rapture and pleasure": there is rapture and there is pleasure.
In this context, what is rapture?
That which is rapture, gladness, rejoicing, rejoicing in, laughter, cheerful laughter, elation, exultation, mental buoyancy, and satisfaction of mind—
this is called “rapture.
In this context, what is pleasure?
That which is mental ease, mental pleasure, the pleasant and pleasurable feeling born of mental contact, the pleasant and pleasurable sensation born of mental contact—
this is called "pleasure. This pleasure is accompanied by, co-arisen with, conjoined with, and associated with this rapture (pīti).
Therefore it is called "rapture and happiness.
"First" means first in the sequence of counting;
it is called "first" because this is the first [jhāna] one attains.
“Jhāna” means applied thought (vitakka), sustained thought (vicāra), rapture (pīti), pleasure (sukha), and one-pointedness of mind (cittassekaggatā).
“Having attained” (upasampajja) means the gaining, obtaining, reaching, achieving, touching, realizing, and full attainment of the first jhāna.
“Dwells” (viharati) … [and so on] …
Therefore it is said, "he dwells.
Regarding the phrase "with the subsiding of applied thought and sustained thought": there is applied thought, there is sustained thought.
In this context, what is applied thought?
Whatever is thought, initial application of thought ... pe ... right intention—this is called "thought" (vitakka).
In this context, what is sustained application of thought (vicāra)?

Whatever is initial mental application, sustained mental application, close mental application, and detailed mental application— the state of the mind’s continuous engagement and its repeated examination—
this is called "sustained mental application" (vicāra). Thus,

this initial mental application and this sustained mental application become stilled, calmed, subsided, brought to an end, vanished, settled, thoroughly settled, dried up, completely dried up, and brought to an end.
Therefore it is said: “With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought.
“Internally” means that which is internal and personal.
“Tranquility” means faith, believing, conviction, and full confidence.
“Unification of mind” is that stability of the mind … right concentration.
“Without applied thought and without sustained thought”: there is applied thought, there is sustained thought.
In this context, what is applied thought?
Whatever is reasoning, initial application of the mind … up to … right intention—
this is called "initial application" (vitakka).
In this context, what is sustained application (vicāra)?

Whatever is moving, following movement, sustained movement, thorough investigation, mental exploration, the continuous threading of the mind, and the constant scrutiny of it— this is called "sustained thought" (vicāra). Thus,

this initial thought (vitakka) and this sustained thought (vicāra) become stilled, calmed, subsided, come to an end, passed away, settled, thoroughly settled, dried up, completely dried up, and brought to an end.
Therefore it is said, "without initial application and without sustained application.
"Born of concentration" refers to serenity, rapture, and happiness;
these have arisen, been produced, come into being, been fully manifested, and become apparent within this concentration.
Therefore it is called "born of concentration.
Regarding "joy and bliss": there is joy, and there is bliss.
Therein, what is joy? ... [as before] ...
This is called "rapture.
In that regard, what is "happiness"? ... [as before] ...
this is called "happiness."
This happiness is accompanied by, co-nascent with, conjoined with, and associated with this rapture.
Therefore it is called "rapture-and-happiness.
"Second" means second in the numerical sequence.
It is called "the second" because one enters upon it as the second.
"Jhāna" refers to serenity, rapture and pleasure, and one-pointedness of mind.
"Having attained" (upasampajja) means the obtaining, the acquisition, the reaching, the achievement, the touching, the realization, and the full attainment of the second jhāna.
“He dwells”: ... [as before] ...
therefore it is said, “he dwells.
Regarding the phrase “with the fading away of rapture,” therein, what is rapture?
That which is rapture, gladness, rejoicing, delight, laughter, mirth, elation, exultation, mental buoyancy, and satisfaction of mind—
this is called "rapture. This rapture becomes calmed,
stilled, subsided, passed away, utterly passed away, allayed, thoroughly allayed, dried up, completely dried up, and brought to an end.
Therefore it is said, "and with the fading away of rapture.
Regarding the term "equanimous": what therein is equanimity?
It is that which is equanimity, the act of being equanimous, the state of looking on with equanimity, and mental neutrality.
This is called "equanimity.
One is endowed with this equanimity... [as before] ...possessed of it.
Therefore, one is called "equanimous."
“He dwells” (*viharati*) … [as before] … therefore it is said, “he dwells.
Regarding the phrase “mindful and clearly comprehending” (*sato ca sampajāno*): therein, what is mindfulness (*sati*)?
That which is mindfulness, recollection... [and so on] ...right mindfulness—this is called “mindfulness.
In this context, what is clear comprehension?
That wisdom which is understanding ... [as above] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view—this is called "clear comprehension.
Thus, he is endowed with this mindfulness and this clear comprehension ... [as above] ... possessed of them.
Therefore it is said, “mindful and clearly comprehending.
Regarding the phrase, “he experiences pleasure with the body,” what therein is pleasure?
That which is mental satisfaction, mental pleasure, the pleasant and pleasurable feeling born of mind-contact—that is, the pleasant and pleasurable sensation born of mind-contact.
This is called "pleasure.
In that context, what is the body?
It is the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness.
This is called "the body.
One experiences this pleasure with this body.
Therefore, it is said: "and he experiences pleasure with the body."
Regarding the phrase, “That which the Noble Ones declare”: therein, who are the Noble Ones?
The Noble Ones are said to be the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddhas.
They declare this, teach it, describe it, establish it, reveal it, analyze it, make it plain, and elucidate it.
Therefore it is said: "That which the Noble Ones describe.
Regarding the phrase "equanimous, mindful, dwelling in happiness," what therein is equanimity (*upekkhā*)?
It is that which is equanimity, the act of equanimizing, thorough equanimizing, and mental neutrality.
This is called “equanimity.
In this context, what is mindfulness?
That which is mindfulness, constant mindfulness … [as before] … right mindfulness.
This is called “mindfulness.
In this context, what is pleasure?
That which is mental well-being, mental pleasure, a pleasant and pleasurable feeling born of mind-contact, a pleasant and pleasurable sensation born of mind-contact—this is [pleasure].
This is called "happiness.
Thus, endowed with this equanimity, this mindfulness, and this happiness, one conducts oneself, proceeds, protects, preserves, maintains, moves about, and dwells.
Therefore, it is said: "one who dwells in happiness, mindful and equanimous."
“Third”: it is the third by way of numerical sequence;
it is called the third because one attains this as the third.
“Jhāna”: equanimity, mindfulness, clear comprehension, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind.
“Having attained” (*upasampajja*) means the gaining, obtaining, reaching, achieving, touching, realizing, and full attainment (*upasampadā*) of the third jhāna.
“Dwells” (*viharati*) … [as before] … therefore it is said, “dwells.”
“With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain”: there is pleasure, and there is pain.
In this context, what is pleasure?
That which is bodily ease, bodily pleasure, a pleasant and pleasurable feeling born of body-contact—that is, a pleasant and pleasurable sensation born of body-contact.
This is called "pleasure.
In this context, what is suffering?
That which is bodily displeasure, bodily pain, the unpleasant and painful feeling born of body-contact, the unpleasant and painful sensation born of body-contact—this is suffering.
This is called "suffering.
Thus, this pleasure and this suffering have become stilled, calmed, subsided, passed away, utterly passed away, vanished, disappeared, dried up, completely dried up, and brought to an end.
Therefore it is said: "With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of suffering."
“With the subsiding of both joy and grief beforehand”: there is joy, and there is grief.
In this context, what is joy?
That which is mental ease, mental pleasure, born of mental contact, an agreeable and pleasant experience born of mental contact—an agreeable and pleasant feeling born of mental contact.
This is called "mental joy" (*somanassa*).
In this context, what is "mental grief" (*domanassa*)?
It is that which is mental unease, mental suffering, a disagreeable and painful experience born of mental contact—a disagreeable and painful feeling born of mental contact.
This is called "mental distress.

Thus, this mental joy and this mental distress have previously been stilled, calmed, subsided, passed away, vanished, dissolved, thoroughly dissolved, dried up, completely dried up, and brought to an end.
Therefore it is said: "With the previous disappearance of mental joy and mental distress."

“Neither-painful-nor-pleasant”: that mental state which is neither agreeable nor disagreeable, born of mind-contact, an experience born of mind-contact that is neither painful nor pleasant—that is called “neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Regarding “purity of mindfulness through equanimity,” therein, what is equanimity?
That which is equanimity, the state of being equanimous, thorough equanimity, and mental neutrality—
this is called "equanimity.
In this context, what is mindfulness?
That which is mindfulness, recollection, ... [and so on] ... right mindfulness—this is called "mindfulness.
This mindfulness is opened up, purified, and cleansed by this equanimity.
Therefore it is called “purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
“Fourth”: it is the fourth in the numerical sequence; it is the fourth because one attains this as the fourth.
“Jhāna”: [it consists of] equanimity, mindfulness, and one-pointedness of mind.
“Having attained” (upasampajja) means: the obtaining, the regaining, the reaching, the achievement, the touching, the realization, and the full attainment of the fourth jhāna.
“Dwells” (viharati): ... [as before] ...
therefore it is said, “he dwells.”
“With the complete surmounting of perceptions of form”: therein, what are perceptions of form?

The perception, perceiving, state of having perceived, of one who has attained a fine-material-sphere attainment, or who has been reborn there, or who dwells in happiness in this very life—these are called "perceptions of form."
He has transcended, surpassed, and completely overcome these perceptions of form.
Therefore it is said: "by completely transcending all perceptions of form.
Regarding the phrase "with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance": therein, what are perceptions of resistance?
Perception of forms, perception of sounds, ... pe ...
perception of tangibles—these are called "perceptions of resistance."
These perceptions of resistance have become calm, stilled, subsided, passed away, utterly passed away, dissolved, fully dissolved, withered away, completely withered away, and brought to an end.
Therefore, it is said: "through the passing away of perceptions of resistance.
Regarding the phrase "through non-attention to perceptions of diversity": therein, what are perceptions of diversity?

For one who has not attained [jhāna], whether possessing the mind-element (*manodhātu*) or possessing the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*), perception, perceiving, and the state of having perceived—
these are called "perceptions of diversity.
He does not attend to these perceptions of diversity.
Therefore it is said: “By not attending to perceptions of diversity.
Regarding the phrase “infinite space,” what therein is space?
That which is space, that which has become space, the void, that which has become a void, the opening, that which has become an opening, unimpeded by the four great elements.
This is called "space.
One fixes the mind on that space, steadies it, and pervades it as infinite.
Therefore, it is said: "infinite space."

“‘The base of infinite space’ (ākāsānañcāyatana) refers to the mental states and mental factors of one who has attained the base of infinite space, or one who has been reborn there, or one who dwells in happiness in this very life.
‘Having fully attained’ (upasampajja) means the acquisition, the regaining, the reaching, the achievement, the touching, the realization, and the full attainment of the base of infinite space.
‘Dwells’ (viharati)…” [and so forth].
Therefore it is said, “he dwells.
Regarding the phrase “having completely transcended the base of infinite space”: he has passed beyond, surpassed, and fully transcended this base of infinite space.
Therefore it is said, “having completely transcended the base of infinite space.”
“‘Infinite consciousness’: he attends to that very same space as touched by consciousness and pervades it as infinite.
Therefore it is called ‘infinite consciousness.

‘The base of infinite consciousness’ refers to the states of mind and mental factors of one who has attained the base of infinite consciousness, or one who has been reborn there, or one who dwells in happiness in this very life.”

“Having attained” (*upasampajja*) means: that which is the obtaining, the acquisition, the reaching, the achievement, the touching, the realization, and the full attainment (*upasampadā*) of the base of infinite consciousness.
“Dwells” (*viharati*)...
[as before] ...therefore it is said, “he dwells.”
“Having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness”: he has transcended, surpassed, and fully overcome this base of infinite consciousness.
Therefore it is said, “having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness.
“There is nothing whatsoever”: he develops and dissolves that very same consciousness, making it vanish, and sees, “there is nothing whatsoever.”
Therefore it is said: “There is nothing whatsoever.

“The base of nothingness” refers to the mental states and mental factors of one who has attained the base of nothingness, or one who has been reborn there, or one who dwells in happiness in this very life.
“Having fully entered” means the acquisition, the attainment, the reaching, the achievement, the touching, the realization, and the full entry into the base of nothingness.
“He dwells” (*viharati*)...
[as before] ...therefore it is said, “he dwells.
“Having completely transcended the base of nothingness” means he has passed beyond, surpassed, and fully transcended this base of nothingness.
Therefore it is said: “Having completely transcended the base of nothingness.
One attends to that very base of nothingness as peaceful and develops the attainment with a residue of formations;
therefore it is called “neither-perception-nor-non-perception.”

“Neither-perception-nor-non-perception sphere” (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*) refers to the mental states and mental factors of one who has attained the neither-perception-nor-non-perception sphere, or one who has been reborn there, or one who dwells in happiness in this very life.

“Having fully attained” (*upasampajja*) means the acquisition, the regaining, the reaching, the achievement, the touching, the realization, and the full attainment of the neither-perception-nor-non-perception sphere.
“Dwells” (*viharati*) means he moves about, conducts himself, protects, maintains, sustains, wanders, and abides.
Therefore it is said, “he dwells.
This concludes the Suttantabhājanīya. 2.
The Abhidhammabhājanīya.
2.1. Wholesome States of the Fine-Material Sphere:
The four jhānas—the first jhāna, the second jhāna, the third jhāna, and the fourth jhāna.
In this regard, what is the first jhāna?

Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu, for the sake of rebirth in the realm of form, develops the path, secluded from sensual pleasures... [as before] ...and enters and dwells in the first jhāna based on the earth-kasiṇa, at that time the jhāna possesses five factors:
applied thought (vitakka), sustained thought (vicāra), rapture (pīti), happiness (sukha), and one-pointedness of mind (cittassekaggatā).
This is called the first jhāna.
The remaining phenomena are associated with the jhāna.
In that regard, what is the second jhāna?

Here, bhikkhus, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops the path for rebirth in the form realm, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which possesses the earth-kasiṇa; at that time there is a three-factored jhāna:
rapture, pleasure, and one-pointedness of mind.
This is called the second jhāna.
The remaining factors are associated with jhāna.
Therein, what is the third jhāna?
Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops the path for rebirth in the form realm, through the fading away of rapture … [as before] … this is the third jhāna.
Having attained and dwelled in the third jhāna based on the earth-kasiṇa, at that time there is a two-factored jhāna:
pleasure and one-pointedness of mind.
This is called "the third jhāna."
The remaining factors are associated with jhāna.
Therein, what is the fourth jhāna?

Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops the path for rebirth in the form realm, having abandoned pleasure … [as before] … enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna with the earth-kasiṇa, at that time there is a two-factored jhāna:
Equanimity and one-pointedness of mind:
this is called the fourth jhāna.
The remaining factors are associated with the jhāna.
A Tetrad.

Here, monks, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops the path for rebirth in the form realm, secluded from sensual pleasures... [as before] ...he enters and dwells in the first jhāna based on the earth-kasiṇa; at that time there is five-factored jhāna:
applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind.
This is called the "first jhāna.
The remaining factors are associated with the jhāna.
Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops the path for rebirth in the form realm, being quite secluded from sensual pleasures and secluded from [unwholesome states]...

With the subsiding of applied thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has no applied thought, consists of sustained thought only, and is born of seclusion, filled with rapture and happiness, taking the earth-kasiṇa as its object. At that time, the jhāna possesses four factors:
sustained thought, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind.
This is called the second jhāna.
The remaining states are associated with the jhāna.

Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops the path for rebirth in the form realm, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought … pe … he enters and dwells in the third jhāna based on the earth-kasiṇa; at that time the jhāna has three factors:
Rapture, pleasure, and one-pointedness of mind:
this is called the third jhāna.
The remaining factors are associated with the jhāna.

Here, bhikkhu, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops the path for rebirth in the form realm, through the fading away of rapture... [as before] ...and enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna based on the earth-kasiṇa, at that time the jhāna possesses two factors:
bliss and one-pointedness of mind.
This is called "the fourth jhāna."
The remaining factors are associated with jhāna.

Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops the path for rebirth in the form realm and, with the abandoning of pleasure... [as before] ...enters and dwells in the fifth jhāna based on the earth-kasiṇa, at that time there is a two-factored jhāna:
equanimity and one-pointedness of mind.
This is called the fifth jhāna.
The remaining factors are associated with the jhāna.
This concludes the pentad.
2.2. Wholesome States of the Formless Realm (Arūpāvacara-kusala) At this time, a bhikkhu develops the path for rebirth in the formless realm;

having completely transcended the base of nothingness, he dwells in the fourth jhāna, accompanied by the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, with the abandoning of pleasure … [as before] … [and the abandoning of pain].
He enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna; at that time, the jhāna has two factors:
equanimity and one-pointedness of mind.
This is called the "fourth jhāna."
The remaining states are associated with jhāna.
2.3. Supramundane Wholesome:
The four jhānas—
The first jhāna, the second jhāna, the third jhāna, and the fourth jhāna.
Therein, what is the first jhāna?

Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna that leads to liberation and results in the diminution of the underlying tendencies to views— [...]* *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the full passage continues with the description of the factors of the first jhāna.*
For the sake of abandoning [the hindrances] and for the attainment of the first stage, secluded from sensual pleasures...
he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is difficult to practice and slow in direct knowledge. At that time, there is a five-factored jhāna:
applied thought (vitakka), sustained thought (vicāra), rapture (pīti), bliss (sukha), and one-pointedness of mind (cittassekaggatā).
This is called the first jhāna.
The remaining factors are associated with the jhāna.
In that regard, what is the second jhāna?
Here, bhikkhus, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna that leads to liberation, conduces to the destruction [of the taints],
for the abandoning of views, for the attainment of the first stage— having the subsiding of applied and sustained thought,
... he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which is difficult practice and slow knowledge— at that time his jhāna possesses three factors:
Rapture, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind:
this is called the second jhāna.
All remaining phenomena are associated with the jhāna.
Therein, what is the third jhāna?

Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna that leads to liberation, conduces to the waning of existence, for the abandoning of views and for the attainment of the first stage—having become dispassionate toward rapture… [as before] …he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, which is difficult to practice and slow in direct knowledge; at that time the jhāna consists of two factors:
Pleasure and one-pointedness of mind:
this is called the third jhāna.
The remaining factors are associated with the jhāna.
Therein, what is the fourth jhāna? Here,
at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna— leading to liberation, leading to the waning of existence—
for the abandoning of views and for the attainment of the first stage, with the abandoning of pleasure … [as above] … having entered upon the fourth jhāna.
He dwells with a practice that is painful and slow in direct knowledge; at that time, there is a two-factored jhāna:
equanimity and one-pointedness of mind.
This is called the fourth jhāna.
The remaining factors are associated with jhāna.
This is the tetrad.
Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna that is leading to liberation and conducive to the destruction of acquisitions, [free from] views...
For the sake of abandoning [the hindrances] and for the attainment of the first stage, secluded from sensual pleasures...
he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is difficult to practice and slow in direct knowledge; at that time, the jhāna consists of five factors:
applied thought (vitakka), sustained thought (vicāra), rapture (pīti), bliss (sukha), and one-pointedness of mind (cittassekaggatā).
This is called the "first jhāna.
The remaining factors are associated with the jhāna.
Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna that is leading to liberation and conducive to the diminution of existence, [free from] views...

For the sake of abandoning [the first stage] and for the attainment of the first stage, secluded from sensual pleasures and secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which is without applied thought and with sustained thought only, born of seclusion, filled with rapture and pleasure;
this is a practice that is difficult and slow in direct knowledge. At that time, the jhāna possesses four factors: sustained thought, rapture, pleasure, and one-pointedness of mind.
This is called the second jhāna.
The remaining factors are associated with the jhāna.
Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna that is leading to liberation and conducive to the destruction of acquisitions, [free] from views...

For the sake of abandoning [the first two factors] and for the attainment of the first stage, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, which is difficult to practice and slow in direct knowledge; at that time, the jhāna possesses three factors:
rapture, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind.
This is called the third jhāna.
The remaining factors are associated with the jhāna.
Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna that is leading to liberation and conducive to the destruction of acquisitions, [freeing him] from views...

With the abandoning [of the hindrances] for the sake of attaining the first stage and through the fading away of rapture, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is difficult to practice and slow in direct knowledge; at that time, the jhāna consists of two factors:
bliss and one-pointedness of mind.
This is called the fourth jhāna.
All remaining phenomena are associated with the jhāna.
Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna that is leading to liberation and conducive to the dismantling of the acquisitions of views—

For the sake of abandoning [the first two factors] and for the attainment of the first stage, with the abandoning of pleasure … [as before] … he enters and dwells in the fifth jhāna, which is difficult to practice and slow in direct knowledge; at that time, the jhāna consists of two factors:
equanimity and one-pointedness of mind.
This is called the fifth jhāna.
The remaining states are associated with jhāna.
This concludes the pentad.
2.4. Rūpāvacara-vipāka (Resultants of the Fine-Material Sphere) The four jhānas:
the first jhāna, the second jhāna, the third jhāna, and the fourth jhāna.
In this regard, what is the first *jhāna*?

Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu, for the sake of rebirth in the realm of form, develops the path, secluded from sensual desires ... [as before] ... enters and dwells in the first *jhāna* with the earth-kasiṇa, at that time there is contact ... [as before] ... there is non-distraction.
These states are wholesome.

As a result of having performed and accumulated that very wholesome kamma pertaining to the fine-material sphere, he, secluded from sensual pleasures … [as before] … enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which has the earth-kasiṇa as its object. At that time, there is five-factored jhāna:
applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, pleasure, and one-pointedness of mind.
This is called the first jhāna.
The remaining factors are associated with the jhāna.
Therein, what is the second jhāna?

Here, bhikkhu, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops the path for rebirth in the form realm, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has the earth-kasiṇa as its object; at that time there is contact...
[and so on] ...there is non-distraction.
These states are wholesome.

Through the performance and accumulation of that very same wholesome kamma of the fine-material sphere, there arises its result: with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought... [the second jhāna]...
[the third jhāna]... and so forth.
He enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna …pe… the first jhāna …pe… the fifth jhāna with the earth-kasiṇa; at that time, there is a two-factored jhāna.
Equanimity and one-pointedness of mind:
this is called the fifth jhāna.
The remaining factors are associated with the jhāna... [and so on].
2.5. Ripeness of the Formless Realm (Arūpāvacara-vipāka) At this time,
monks, when a bhikkhu develops the path for rebirth in the formless realm, having completely transcended the base of nothingness,
accompanied by the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, with the abandoning of pleasure … [as before] … he attains and dwells in the fourth [jhāna].
He enters and dwells in jhāna; at that time there is contact … pe … there is non-distraction.
These states are wholesome.
Through having performed and accumulated that very wholesome kamma of the formless sphere, its result is the base of nothingness in every respect.

Having completely transcended the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, with the abandoning of pleasure … [as before] … he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna; at that time, the jhāna possesses two factors:
equanimity and one-pointedness of mind.
This is called the fourth jhāna.
The remaining factors are associated with the jhāna.
2.6. Supramundane Resultant (Lokuttara-vipāka)
There are four jhānas:
the first jhāna, the second jhāna, the third jhāna, and the fourth jhāna.
Therein, what is the first jhāna?

Here, monks, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna that leads to liberation, conduces to the waning of existence, and is for the abandoning of views and the attainment of the first stage—being secluded from sensual pleasures...
[as before] ...he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is difficult to practice and slow in its direct knowledge—at that time there is contact... [as before] ...there is non-distraction.
These states are wholesome.
As the result of having performed and cultivated that very same supramundane wholesome jhāna, secluded from sensual pleasures...
[as before] ...he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is difficult to practice, slow in its direct knowledge, and empty.
At that time, there is five-factored jhāna:
applied thought (vitakka), sustained thought (vicāra), rapture (pīti), bliss (sukha), and one-pointedness of mind (cittassekaggatā).
This is called the "first jhāna."
The remaining factors are associated with jhāna.
Therein, what is the second jhāna?
Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna that is leading to liberation and conducive to the destruction [of the defilements], [free from] views...

For the sake of abandoning [the hindrances] and for the attainment of the first stage, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which is difficult to practice and slow in direct knowledge; at that time there is contact … [and so on] … there is non-distraction.
These states are wholesome.

Through having performed and cultivated that same supramundane wholesome jhāna, as a result [there arises] the fruition: with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought … the second jhāna … the third jhāna … the fourth jhāna … etc.
When one enters and dwells in the first jhāna …pe… the fifth jhāna, which is difficult to practice, slow in direct knowledge, and empty, at that time there is a two-factored jhāna:
equanimity and one-pointedness of mind.
This is called "the fifth jhāna.
The remaining states are associated with jhāna.
2.7. Functional [states] of the sense-sphere and the fine-material sphere.
There are four jhānas:
the first jhāna, the second jhāna, the third jhāna, and the fourth jhāna.
Therein, what is the first jhāna?
Here, bhikkhus, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops a form-sphere jhāna that is functional (kiriya), neither wholesome nor unwholesome, and not the result of kamma,

which is a pleasant dwelling in this very life, secluded from sensual pleasures … [as before] … attaining and dwelling in the first jhāna with the earth-kasiṇa, at that time there is five-factored jhāna:
Initial application, sustained application, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind—
this is called the first jhāna.
The remaining factors are associated with the jhāna.
Therein, what is the second jhāna?

Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops a form-sphere jhāna that is functional (kiriya), neither wholesome nor unwholesome, and not the result of kamma, which is a pleasant dwelling in this very life—namely, the second jhāna [arising] with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought...
[and so on] ...the third jhāna... [and so on].
He enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna …pe… the first jhāna …pe… and the fifth jhāna with the earth-kasiṇa; at that time there is a two-factored jhāna.
Equanimity and one-pointedness of mind:
this is called the fifth jhāna.
All remaining phenomena are associated with the jhāna.
Here, monks, at whatever time a monk develops a formless-sphere jhāna that is functional (kiriya), neither wholesome nor unwholesome, and not the result of kamma—
a dwelling in happiness in this very life— by completely transcending the base of nothingness,
accompanied by the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and with the abandoning of pleasure … [as before] … entering and dwelling in the fourth jhāna.
When he dwells thus, at that time there is a two-factor jhāna:
equanimity and one-pointedness of mind.
This is called the fourth jhāna.
The remaining states are associated with jhāna.
This concludes the Exposition according to the Abhidhamma (Abhidhammabhājanīya). 3.
The Interrogation by Questions (Pañhāpucchaka).
The four jhānas:

Here, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. ... [and so on] ...

With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and mental unification, is without applied and sustained thought, and possesses rapture and pleasure born of concentration. ... [and so on] ...
With the fading away of rapture, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending;
he experiences happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones declare: "He who is equanimous and mindful dwells in happiness. Thus he enters and dwells in the third jhāna...

With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
Of the four jhānas, how many are wholesome, how many unwholesome, and how many indeterminate …pe… how many are with conflict (*saraṇa*), and how many are without conflict (*araṇa*)?
3.1. The Triads:
They may be wholesome, or they may be indeterminate.
The three jhānas—
excluding the pleasure-feeling arisen therein— are associated with pleasant feeling; the fourth jhāna—
excluding the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arisen therein— is associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
They may be results; they may be states subject to result; they may be neither results nor states subject to result.
They may be acquired and subject to grasping; they may be unacquired but subject to grasping; they may be neither acquired nor subject to grasping.
They may be undefiled but subject to defilement; they may be neither defiled nor subject to defilement.

The first jhāna—excluding the applied thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra) that have arisen therein—it is with applied thought and sustained thought; the [remaining] three jhānas are without applied thought and without sustained thought.
Two jhānas—
Excluding the joy arisen therein, there are three jhānas accompanied by joy;
excluding the bliss arisen therein, there is the fourth jhāna accompanied by bliss;
and excluding the equanimity arisen therein, there is that which is accompanied by equanimity.
They are neither to be abandoned by vision nor by cultivation.
They do not have roots that are to be abandoned either by vision or by cultivation.
They may be leading to accumulation, they may be leading to diminution, or they may be leading neither to accumulation nor to diminution.
They may be of those in training (sekha), they may be of those beyond training (asekha), or they may be neither of those in training nor beyond training.
They may be exalted (mahaggata) or they may be immeasurable (appamāṇa).

Regarding the first three jhānas, they should not be said to have a limited object (parittārammaṇa), nor should they be said to have an exalted object; they may have an immeasurable object, or they may not be said to have an immeasurable object.
The fourth jhāna may have a limited object, it may have a sublime object, or it may have an immeasurable object;
or it may be such that it cannot be said to have a limited object, nor a sublime object, nor an immeasurable object.
It may be mediocre, or it may be excellent.
They may be fixed in rightness, or they may be unfixed.

The first three jhānas do not have the Path as their object; they may have the Path as their cause, or they may have the Path as their predominance, or they should not be described as either "having the Path as their cause" or "having the Path as their predominance.

The fourth jhāna may have the Path as its object, it may have the Path as its cause, or it may have the Path as its predominance; or it should not be described as "having the Path as its object," "having the Path as its cause," or "having the Path as its predominance."
They may have arisen, they may not have arisen, or they may be in the process of arising.
They may be past, they may be future, or they may be present.
The three jhānas should not be described as having a past object, nor as having a future object, nor as having a present object.
The fourth jhāna may have a past object, may have a future object, may have a present object, or it may not be described as having either a past object, a future object, or a present object.
It may be internal, external, or both internal and external.
The first three jhānas have external objects; the fourth jhāna may have an internal object or it may have an external object.
It may have an internal-external object; it may not be described as having an internal object, nor as having an external object, nor as having an internal-external object.
It is non-demonstrable and non-reacting.
3.2. The Dyads:

Those that are not roots, those that are accompanied by roots, and those associated with roots; they should not be called "both roots and accompanied by roots," but rather "accompanied by roots but not roots";
they should not be called "both roots and associated with roots," but rather "associated with roots..."
They are not causes, nor are they accompanied by causes. They have conditions; they are conditioned;
they are non-demonstrable, non-reactive, and formless. They may be mundane or supramundane; they may be cognizable by someone or not cognizable by anyone. They are not taints (*āsava*);

they may be associated with taints or dissociated from taints. They should not be described as "both taints and associated with taints. They may be associated with taints but not themselves taints, or they may not be described as "associated with taints but not themselves taints."
They should not be described as "both taints and associated with taints," nor as "associated with taints but not themselves taints.
They may be dissociated from taints and subject to taints, or they may be dissociated from taints and free from taints.
They are not fetters... [and so on].
There are no fetters … [and so on] … no floods … [and so on] … no bonds … [and so on] …
They are not hindrances ... [and so on] ...

they are not misapprehensions ... [and so on] ... they have an object; they are not consciousness; they are mental factors; they are associated with consciousness; they are conjoined with consciousness; they are generated by consciousness.

They are co-existent with consciousness, following after consciousness, conjoined with and produced by consciousness; they are conjoined with, produced by, and co-existent with consciousness, and follow after consciousness that is conjoined with and produced by consciousness.
They are external, not derived; they may be clung-to, or they may not be clung-to. They are not objects of clinging ... [and so forth].
There are no defilements ... [as above] ...
not to be abandoned by vision, not to be abandoned by cultivation, not having roots to be abandoned by vision, and not having roots to be abandoned by cultivation.
The first jhāna—
Excluding the applied thought (vitakka) arisen therein, the three jhānas are without applied thought (avitakka).
Excluding the sustained thought (vicāra) arisen in the first jhāna, the [remaining] three jhānas are without sustained thought (avicāra).
Two jhānas:
with rapture, excluding the rapture arisen therein; two jhānas are without rapture.
Two jhānas—
Excluding the joy arisen therein, two jhānas are accompanied by joy; [the remaining] two jhānas are not accompanied by joy.
Three jhānas—excluding the bliss arisen therein—are accompanied by bliss; the fourth jhāna is not accompanied by bliss.
The fourth jhāna—excluding the equanimity arisen therein, the three jhānas are accompanied by equanimity;
they are not of the sense sphere, they may be of the fine-material sphere, or they may not be of the fine-material sphere; the three jhānas are not of the immaterial sphere; the fourth [jhāna]...
Jhāna may be immaterial-sphere (arūpāvacara), it may not be immaterial-sphere; it may be included (pariyāpanna), it may be unincluded (apariyāpanna);

it may be leading out (niyyānika), it may not be leading out; it may be fixed (niyata), it may be unfixed (aniyata); it may be surpassable (sauttara), it may be unsurpassable (anuttara); it is without conflict (araṇa). This concludes the section of questions.
The Analysis of the Meditative Absorptions (Jhānavibhaṅga) is finished.
